extracted.intended_audience: crisis managers, public relations practitioners, students and scholars of crisis communication
extracted.subtask_description: Use Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT) to assess crisis responsibility, crisis history, and prior relational reputation to select evidence-based communication strategies (deny, diminish, rebuild, bolstering) that protect organizational reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing and adjusting information for low-responsibility crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Informing and adjusting information alone can be enough when crises have minimal attributions of crisis responsibility (victim crises), no history of similar crises and a neutral or positive prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the organization is perceived as a victim, there is no history of similar crises, and prior relationship reputation is neutral/positive. Focus on providing facts and corrective information rather than admission of fault or large remedial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use victimage for certain victim-type crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Victimage can be used as part of the response for workplace violence, product tampering, natural disasters and rumors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include messages that portray the organization as also harmed by the event (victim) when appropriate—useful for external-cause crises to engender sympathy. Must be credible and supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish strategies when victim crises have history or bad reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies should be used for crises with minimal attributions of crisis responsibility (victim crises) coupled with a history of similar crises and/or negative prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a victim crisis occurs but the organization has prior similar incidents or poor relational history, employ diminish tactics (e.g., excuse, justification) to downplay organizational responsibility while acknowledging concern; reinforce with credible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish strategies for some accident crises with neutral/positive history
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies should be used for crises with low attributions of crisis responsibility (accident crises), which have no history of similar crises, and a neutral or positive prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For accidental crises with little assigned blame and a good past record, use diminish tactics to minimize perceived responsibility and perceived damage—but back claims with credible evidence to avoid losing credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild strategies for accident crises with history or negative reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies should be used for crises with low attributions of crisis responsibility (accident crises), coupled with a history of similar crises and/or negative prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accidents occur but the organization has a history or bad reputation, take stronger remedial actions (compensation, apology) to repair reputation—show tangible corrective measures and acceptance of responsibility where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild strategies for crises with strong attributions (preventable/intentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies should be used for crises with strong attributions of crisis responsibility (preventable crises) regardless of crisis history or prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For crises where the organization is clearly responsible (intentional/preventable), use rebuild approaches (apology, compensation, corrective action) to accept responsibility and seek forgiveness; immediate, sincere remediation is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny posture for rumors and challenge crises when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The deny posture crisis response strategies should be used for rumor and challenge crises, when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If credible evidence shows no organizational involvement (e.g., false rumors), use denial strategies to sever the perceived link between organization and crisis; ensure factual support because unsuccessful denials damage credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency in crisis response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistency in crisis response strategies. Mixing deny crisis response strategies with either the diminish or rebuild strategies will erode the effectiveness of the overall response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflicting messages (e.g., simultaneously denying and apologizing). Choose a coherent posture aligned with attribution level, history, and reputation; inconsistent frames undermine credibility and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess reputational threat using three elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputational threat is influenced by three elements: (1) initial crisis responsibility, (2) crisis history and (3) prior relational reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis managers must evaluate how much stakeholders attribute the crisis to the organization (initial responsibility), whether similar crises have occurred (history), and how the organization has treated stakeholders before (prior relational reputation). These determine likely reputational damage and appropriate strategy selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify crises into victim, accidental, or intentional clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Three crisis clusters: victim cluster (organization also a victim; weak attributions = mild reputational threat), accidental cluster (organizational actions unintentional; minimal attributions = moderate threat), intentional cluster (organization knowingly placed people at risk or violated norms; strong attributions = severe reputational threat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cluster classification to predict attributions of responsibility and choose response type. Examples: victim—natural disaster, rumor, product tampering; accidental—technical-error accidents; intentional—organizational misdeeds, management misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis history and prior relational reputation intensify attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an organization has a history of facing similar crises or a poor history of dealing with stakeholders, attributions of crisis responsibility and the level of reputational threat are greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical patterns and relationship quality escalate stakeholder blame; even low-responsibility incidents can become high-threat if history or relational reputation is negative. Factor this into strategy choice (lean toward rebuild if history/reputation poor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary response strategies (deny, diminish, rebuild)
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT identifies three primary groups of responses: deny (sever perceived connection), diminish (assure publics crisis is not as bad or organization had little control), and rebuild (offer aid/ask forgiveness to change perceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select one primary group based on attribution level and history. Deny is appropriate when organization truly not involved; diminish when responsibility/intent are low; rebuild when responsibility is strong or history/reputation dictates. Each primary group contains specific tactics that should be credible and evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny strategies and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Deny crisis response strategies: Attack the accuser (confront claimant), Denial (assert no crisis), Scapegoat (blame outside person/group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only when supported by facts. Attacking accusers or scapegoating can backfire if evidence contradicts the claims. Deny works best for rumors or externally-caused incidents accepted by media/stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish strategies and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies: Excuse (minimize responsibility by denying intent or claiming inability to control events), Justification (minimize perceived damage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide credible evidence to support minimization claims. Overuse or weak evidence for excuses/justifications reduces credibility. Use to reframe severity or intent when blame is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild strategies and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies: Compensation (offer money or gifts to victims), Apology (indicate full responsibility and ask forgiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responsibility is high, provide tangible remediation and sincere apologies. Rebuild strategies aim to change stakeholders' perceptions through action and contrition; follow-through on promises is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolstering (secondary) strategies and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary crisis response strategies—Bolstering: Reminder (tell stakeholders about past good works), Ingratiation (praise stakeholders or remind them of past good works), Victimage (remind stakeholders the organization is a victim too).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolstering attempts to increase positive perceptions and sympathy. Coombs warns bolstering should supplement primary responses, not replace them. Use carefully to avoid appearing manipulative or as a diversion from responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media framing and the importance of placing the organization's frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Each strategy helps the organization get its side of the story into the media; how the crisis is framed in the media will determine how the organization's publics view the situation. The media's frames become the stakeholders’ frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis managers must proactively communicate to influence media frames; if media frames conflict, stakeholders will adopt the frame from the most credible source. Ensure messages are consistent, supported by evidence, and delivered by credible spokespeople.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of crisis response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis response strategies have three objectives relative to protecting reputations: (1) shape attributions of the crisis, (2) change perceptions of the organization in crisis and (3) reduce the negative effect generated by the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning responses, evaluate whether chosen messages and actions will (a) influence who is blamed, (b) alter stakeholder perceptions of the organization, and (c) mitigate adverse consequences. Use these objectives as criteria for strategy selection and evaluation.
